guidance.title: The Basics - what a weight tolerance actually is
guidance.content:
The Basics — what a weight tolerance actually is
Section 01 · Why a "100 g" weight is not exactly 100 g, and why that matters
A "calibration weight" (or test mass) is a piece of metal — typically stainless steel — manufactured to be very close to a specific nominal value. You use it to
calibrate or verify a balance: place a 100 g weight on the pan, the balance should read 100.000 g, and if it does not, you adjust the balance until it does. But
that "100 g" weight is not exactly 100.0000000 g. No physical object can be made to perfect exactness. The weight's actual mass falls within a permitted
range — and that range is its tolerance.
THE KEY IDEA
Tolerance = the maximum amount a calibration weight is allowed to differ from its nominal value while still being sold under that class.
A 100 g weight rated to ASTM Class 1 must have an actual mass between 99.99975 g and 100.00025 g (a tolerance of ±0.25 mg).
A 100 g weight rated to ASTM Class 4 only needs to be within 100.000 g ± 2 mg — much looser.
The simple framing
— Tighter class = smaller tolerance = more expensive weight.
— Looser class = bigger tolerance = cheaper weight.
— Match the class to the balance's precision. Don't go looser. Going tighter is fine but costs more.

guidance.title: Tolerance vs. Uncertainty
guidance.content:
Tolerance vs. Uncertainty
Section 02 · Two concepts that get confused — they are not the same thing
Tolerance — what is allowed
Tolerance is the manufacturing specification. ASTM Class 1 says: "any weight we sell as a 100 g Class 1 will be within ±0.25 mg of nominal." You buy by
tolerance.
Uncertainty — what is measured
Uncertainty is what you find when you actually calibrate that specific weight against a reference standard. The calibration certificate that ships with a high-
class weight reports both the measured mass and a statistical uncertainty — typically much smaller than the tolerance.
A WORKED EXAMPLE
You buy a 100 g ASTM Class 1 calibration weight.
Tolerance (the spec): ±0.25 mg. The weight is permitted to be anywhere from 99.99975 g to 100.00025 g.
Calibration certificate (the measurement): "Conventional mass = 100.00018 g, expanded uncertainty (k=2) = ±0.04 mg."
In practice, the actual mass is known to ±0.04 mg — six times tighter than the tolerance allows.
When to use which
— Use TOLERANCE when buying or specifying a weight, when matching a class to a balance, or when you are not using a calibration certificate.
— Use UNCERTAINTY when you have a calibrated weight with a certificate and need the most accurate reference value possible.

guidance.title: Maximum Permissible Error (MPE)
guidance.content:
Maximum Permissible Error (MPE)
Section 03 · A third vocabulary word, and the two-scopes problem that makes it confusing
MPE is OIML's formal term for "the largest error something is allowed to have." It is used in two different scopes that share the same name: MPE of a weight
(= tolerance), and MPE of a balance (a separate concept defined by OIML R 76).
MPE of a weight = tolerance
When OIML R 111 specifies the limits for a calibration weight, it calls those limits "Maximum Permissible Errors." That is the same concept ASTM E617 calls
"tolerance." Identical idea, different vocabulary. "OIML F1, 100 g, MPE ±0.5 mg" and "tolerance ±0.5 mg" describe the same limit.
MPE of a balance = a separate concept (OIML R 76)
When OIML R 76 specifies the limits for a non-automatic weighing instrument, the same term "MPE" applies — but now it describes how much error the
balance itself is allowed to have during weighing. It is expressed in scale divisions (d) and grows with the load placed on the balance. Balances are graded
into Roman-numeral classes I, II, III, and IIII.
Balance Class Typical use Low-load MPE Medium-load MPE High-load MPE
I Special accuracy Analytical / lab balances ±0.5 d (0 – 50 000 d) ±1.0 d (to 200 000 d) ±1.5 d (above)
II High accuracy Precision / commercial labs ±0.5 d (0 – 5 000 d) ±1.0 d (to 20 000 d) ±1.5 d (above)
III Medium accuracy Commercial / legal-for-trade scales ±0.5 d (0 – 500 d) ±1.0 d (to 2 000 d) ±1.5 d (above)
IIII Ordinary Coarse industrial scales ±0.5 d (0 – 50 d) ±1.0 d (to 200 d) ±1.5 d (above)
TWO ROMAN-NUMERAL SYSTEMS — DON'T CONFUSE THEM
Weight classes: E1 · E2 · F1 · F2 · M1 · M2 · M3 (describe the WEIGHT)
Balance classes: I · II · III · IIII (describe the BALANCE)
A "Class III balance" calibrated with "Class F2 weights" is a normal pairing. The two systems are independent — same Roman numerals, different meaning.

guidance.title: The Two Class Systems - ASTM E617 vs. OIML R 111
guidance.content:
The Two Class Systems — ASTM E617 vs. OIML R 111
Section 04 · Both standards are quoted on OHAUS service manuals; they run in parallel
ASTM E617 (the American system)
Published by ASTM International. Classes are numbered 000, 00, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Lower number = tighter tolerance. Most common in laboratory work
and in OHAUS manuals: Class 1 (analytical), Class 4 (industrial bench), Class F (commercial scales — see note below).
OIML R 111 (the international system)
Published by the International Organization of Legal Metrology. Classes are letter-coded: E1, E2, F1, F2, M1, M2, M3. "E" = highest precision (Electronic
balance), "F" = mid (Field-grade), "M" = lowest precision (Mechanical scale). E1 is tightest, M3 is loosest.
Rough cross-mapping
ASTM E617 OIML R 111 Typical use
Class 0 OIML E1 Reference standards, high-precision balances
Class 1 OIML E2 Analytical balances (0.0001 g readability)
Class 2 OIML F1 Precision balances (0.001 g readability)
Class 3 / 4 OIML F2 Precision / industrial balances (0.01 – 0.1 g)
Class 5 / 6 OIML M1 Industrial scales (1 – 10 g readability)
Class 7 OIML M2 / M3 Field / commercial scales
A NOTE ON "ASTM CLASS F"
You will see "ASTM Class F" in OHAUS service manuals (especially Defender and Courier). ASTM E617 does not actually have a Class F.
"Class F" refers to NIST Handbook 44 Class F — an American legal-metrology class for commercial / legal-for-trade scales. Separate system from ASTM E617.
In practice, "ASTM Class F or OIML M1" is the standard wording for industrial-scale calibration weights and is widely understood, even if it technically mixes two
systems.

guidance.title: Tolerance Values at Common Masses
guidance.content:
Tolerance Values at Common Masses
Section 05 · Real numbers from the published Troemner tables (ASTM E617 and OIML R 111)
Tolerance always grows with nominal mass — a 1 kg weight has a larger absolute tolerance than a 1 g weight in the same class. Values below are pulled
directly from the Troemner published reference tables.
ASTM E617 — selected classes (tolerance in mg)
Nominal Class 0 Class 1 Class 2 Class 3 Class 4 Class 6
1 g 0.017 0.034 0.054 0.10 0.20 2.0
10 g 0.025 0.050 0.074 0.25 0.50 2.0
100 g 0.13 0.25 0.50 1.0 2.0 10
1 kg 1.3 2.5 5.0 10 20 100
10 kg 13 25 50 100 200 1 000
OIML R 111 — selected classes (tolerance in mg)
Nominal E1 E2 F1 F2 M1 M2
1 g 0.010 0.03 0.10 0.30 1.0 3.0
10 g 0.020 0.06 0.20 0.60 2.0 6.0
100 g 0.05 0.16 0.50 1.6 5.0 16
1 kg 0.50 1.6 5.0 16 50 160
10 kg 5.0 16 50 160 500 1 600
Source: Troemner Calibration Weight Tolerance Reference (troemner.com). All values in milligrams. ASTM Class 1 "H OIML E2 at high masses but is tighter than E2 at 1 g — the systems are not
exact numerical equivalents.

guidance.title: Which Class Do I Need? - OHAUS Cross-Reference
guidance.content:
Which Class Do I Need? — OHAUS Cross-Reference
Section 06 · Same recommendations that appear on each series' divider page in this document
Match the calibration weight class to your balance's accuracy tier. The table below lists the OHAUS recommendation for each balance series — the same
values shown on the section divider chips throughout this Master Reference.
Balance Series Readability tier ASTM OIML
Adventurer AX Semi-micro / 0.00001 g Class 1 E1
Explorer EX, EXP, EXR Analytical / 0.0001 g Class 1 E2
Pioneer (PA / PR / PJX) Analytical / 0.0001 g Class 1 E2
Scout (STX / SKX / SPX / SJX) Precision / 0.001 g Class 1 E2
Moisture analyzers (MB family) 0.001 g Class 1 E2
Navigator (NV / NVT / NVHD) 0.01 – 1 g Class 4 F2
Valor (V12P – V7000) 0.1 – 5 g Class 4 F2
Compass (CR / CX) 0.1 – 1 g Class 4 F2
Traveler (TA / TAJ / TAG / SE) 0.001 – 1 g Class 4 F2
Defender bench / pallet (B-V, F) 5 – 50 g Class 4 F2
Defender industrial / Courier 0.005 – 0.1 kg Class F (NIST) M1
THE PRACTICAL RULE
Going TIGHTER than the recommendation is fine — a Class 1 weight will work on a Defender; it just costs more.
Going LOOSER than the recommendation injects error. Do not use a Class 4 weight to calibrate an analytical balance.
When in doubt, look at the balance's smallest division (the d value). The cal-weight tolerance should be smaller than that division.

guidance.title: The 1/3 Rule + Worked Examples
guidance.content:
The 1/3 Rule + Worked Examples
Section 07 · How to verify your chosen class is appropriate for the balance you are calibrating
A common rule of thumb: a calibration weight's tolerance should be no larger than one-third of the balance's smallest division (its readability, d). This keeps
the weight's contribution to total measurement error well below the balance's own measurement noise.
THE 1/3 RULE
Cal-weight tolerance <= (1 / 3) × balance readability
If the balance reads to 0.0001 g (0.1 mg), the cal-weight tolerance should be at most 0.033 mg.
If the balance reads to 0.01 g (10 mg), the cal-weight tolerance should be at most 3.3 mg.
Worked example — Adventurer AX analytical balance
AX-series readability is 0.0001 g (= 0.1 mg). One-third of that is ~0.033 mg. So the 100 g calibration weight needs a tolerance no larger than 0.033 mg.
Class Tolerance @ 100 g <= 0.033 mg? Verdict
ASTM Class 0 0.13 mg NO (0.13 > 0.033) Too loose by 1/3 rule
ASTM Class 00 0.05 mg NO (0.05 > 0.033) Borderline — does not pass strict rule
ASTM Class 000 0.025 mg YES (0.025 < 0.033) Passes — but very expensive
OIML E1 0.05 mg NO (0.05 > 0.033) Borderline
In practice, the strict 1/3 rule is hard to satisfy at the very top of the precision pyramid. OHAUS recommends ASTM Class 1 / OIML E1 for AX-series —
pragmatic, accepts a slightly larger contribution from the cal weight in exchange for reasonable cost.
Worked example — Defender industrial scale
Defender industrial scales typically have 0.005 kg (5 g) readability. One-third is 1.7 g = 1700 mg — plenty of headroom. Class 4 weights (tolerance 2 mg at
100 g) easily satisfy the 1/3 rule. OHAUS recommends Class F / OIML M1 for industrial bases, well within the rule.

guidance.title: Quick Reference & Glossary
guidance.content:
Quick Reference & Glossary
Section 08 · Compact lookup of the vocabulary used in this appendix
In one sentence
A calibration weight's class tells you how close to nominal it actually is — tighter classes (Class 1, E1) cost more and let you calibrate more precise
balances; looser classes (Class 4, F2, M1) are fine for industrial scales.
Glossary
Term Definition
Calibration weight A reference mass used to calibrate or verify a balance/scale. Same as "test mass."
Tolerance The maximum amount a calibration weight is allowed to differ from its nominal value while still being sold under its class.
OIML's formal term for "largest error allowed." For weights, MPE = tolerance. For balances, MPE is what the balance itself is
Maximum Permissible Error (MPE)
allowed to be off — specified in scale divisions, grows with load.
OIML R 76 grading of weighing instruments: I (analytical), II (precision), III (commercial / LFT), IIII (coarse industrial). Different
Balance accuracy class
from weight classes.
Statistical uncertainty in the calibrated mass of a specific weight, reported on its certificate. Usually much smaller than
Uncertainty
tolerance.
Class A precision tier defined by a standards body. Tells you the tolerance.
ASTM E617 American standard. Numbered classes 000 – 7 — lower is tighter.
OIML R 111 International standard. Letter-coded E1 – M3 — E1 tightest, M3 loosest.
NIST Class F American legal-for-trade class for commercial scales. Often informally called "ASTM Class F" in OHAUS manuals.
Nominal value The marked label value of the weight (e.g., "100 g"). Actual mass is within nominal ± tolerance.

guidance.title: 1/3 Rule and Conventional Mass
guidance.content:
1/3 rule Practical guideline: cal-weight tolerance should be at most one-third of the balance's smallest division.
Mass value reported on a calibration certificate, calculated under standard reference conditions (8000 kg/m³ density, 20 °C
Conventional mass
air).
